capabilities.target: Postgres database via Supabase service role, bypasses row level security, can read any table including integration_tokens
support_messages table, rows rendered back to the customer in the ticket thread

inputs.source: Developer's instruction typed into the IDE chat
Customer-authored ticket message submitted through the public support widget, stored in support_messages and later read back by the agent

instructions.evidence_locator: runtime notes: "database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security"
instructions.note: No declared instruction or technical boundary restricts execute_sql to ticket-related tables for a ticket-browsing task; the same broad credential can reach a table of integration tokens in response to a one-line developer request.

elements.name: integration_tokens table, readable by the service role which bypasses row level security
support_messages table; rows are rendered back to the customer in the ticket UI
@supabase/mcp-server-supabase, launched via npx -y with an unpinned @latest tag
stdio connection from the IDE agent to the Supabase MCP server, carrying the service role PAT

controls.name: Per-call human approval showing raw SQL (IDE client confirmation prompt)
controls.decay_rationale: The approver sees the literal SQL for each call (raw_action), not a model-written summary, so a more capable model cannot change what is displayed. It is not defeated by model capability; it is defeated by volume (approval fatigue) and by splitting one malicious sequence across several individually unremarkable calls -- the runtime notes state developers already 'approve many calls in a session,' which is direct evidence this gate is read quickly rather than audited line by line.

controls.name: Least-privilege, RLS-respecting credential for the agent's database connection
controls.decay_rationale: A connection that cannot read integration_tokens (or any secrets table) makes that read impossible regardless of what the model is instructed to do, including by injected content.

controls.name: Content/DLP filter on inserts to customer-visible tables
controls.decay_rationale: Pattern matching on secret-shaped strings can be evaded by encoding, splitting, or paraphrasing the value being exfiltrated, so it narrows the path rather than closing it.

controls.name: Pin the Supabase MCP server to a specific, hash-verified release
controls.decay_rationale: Does not decay with model capability. Removes the unreviewed-update vector a rug pull depends on, since a new malicious release is not fetched automatically.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) with confused deputy (TC4): ticket injection + service-role read of credentials + reply egress to the customer

attack_path.note: Customer submits a support ticket containing hidden instructions (indirect prompt injection), stored in support_messages.
Developer asks the agent to show open tickets; the agent runs execute_sql with the service role and loads ticket content, including the injected instructions, into its context.
Following the injected instructions, the agent issues a further execute_sql read against integration_tokens, which the service role can reach because it bypasses row level security.
The agent inserts a reply into support_messages containing the harvested token values; this row is rendered back to the customer, completing exfiltration to the attacker.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: An 'auto-approve' or 'trust this workspace' setting appears in the IDE client that skips per-call confirmation, the approval gate is narrowed or disabled, or the median number of approvals per developer session keeps rising (already described as 'many calls in a session').

evidence.observation: "The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security. A table of integration tokens sits in the same database." -- confirms a single broad credential reaches both ticket data and a credentials table.

"Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget. Rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer." -- confirms support_messages is both an untrusted inbound channel and an egress channel visible to the same external party.

"The IDE client asks the developer to approve each tool call and shows the SQL. Developers approve many calls in a session." -- confirms a raw_action approval gate exists, but also supplies the volume evidence used to justify adding longer_task_horizon as a forecast trigger for this gate.
Developer's prompt is a one-line, unscoped request ("Show me the latest open support tickets"), with no stated instruction limiting which tables the agent may subsequently query.

recommendations.action: Scope the agent's database connection to a role that respects row level security and cannot read the integration_tokens table (or any secrets table) at all.
Add a content/DLP filter on inserts to support_messages that blocks secret-shaped strings (API keys, JWTs, connection strings) before the write executes.

Make the approval prompt flag when a proposed query touches tables outside the ticket/support domain (e.g. integration_tokens), so cross-table access is visually distinct from routine ticket read/reply calls, instead of relying on the developer recognizing intent from raw SQL text alone.
Add an explicit instruction that ticket message content is untrusted data and must never be treated as a command to the agent.

findings.title: Unpinned MCP server package enables silent tool redefinition (ASI04 rug pull)

attack_path.note: Server is launched via `npx -y @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest`, fetching whatever version is currently published with no pin or hash check.
A compromised or rug-pulled release could redefine tool descriptions or schemas to direct the agent to read sensitive tables under the same service-role credential.
...and exfiltrate results through the same customer-visible reply path as finding F1.

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: Same signal as F1: the shared per-call approval gate being narrowed, disabled, or routinely rubber-stamped is what turns a supply-chain compromise of this server into a completed exfiltration.

evidence.observation: `["-y", "@supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest", "--access-token", "${SUPABASE_PAT}"]` -- the `@latest` tag and `npx -y` mean the exact package version and its tool definitions are not pinned or hash-verified before each run.

recommendations.action: Pin the MCP server to an exact version with a verified checksum or lockfile entry, and review diffs before upgrading.
Log and diff the MCP server's advertised tool list and schemas between sessions, and alert on any change.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: an untrusted customer can write ticket content that a service-role database credential (which bypasses row level security and sits in the same database as a table of integration tokens) can be induced to read, and the only outbound channel available (inserting a reply into support_messages) is rendered straight back to that same customer -- a complete lethal-trifecta path (TC1) compounded by a confused-deputy credential (TC4). An unpinned MCP server package (@latest, no hash) adds a second, independent route to the same sinks (ASI04). The one declared control, a per-call approval prompt that shows raw SQL, is credited per rubric section 5 step 2 (-2 tiers, floor waived because review mode is raw_action), giving a residual of moderate for both findings. That credit is optimistic: the same artifact that describes the gate also states developers 'approve many calls in a session,' which is the condition under which raw-action approval gates degrade (approval fatigue, SAFE-T1403 / ASI09), and the malicious sequence here is naturally split into individually unremarkable calls (read tickets; read a table; insert a reply) rather than one obviously dangerous action. Because this single gate is the only thing holding the tier down, and it is already shown to run at high volume, the forecast reverts to critical under autonomy_increase, control_removal, or continued growth in session length (longer_task_horizon) -- the control whose decay drives the forecast is ctl.tool_call_prompt. No structural control currently prevents the service-role connection from reading the integration_tokens table or prevents secret-shaped content from being written into a customer-visible row; both are recommended as p1 structural fixes.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior; no logs, traces, or live tests of the approval prompt or the MCP server's actual tool definitions were available.

No system prompt or agent instructions were provided beyond the one-line developer request, so instruction review is limited to what the runtime notes imply; this lowers confidence on the 'instructions' findings.

The exact row level security policies, table schema, and whether integration_tokens is reachable from the same connection used for ticket tables are inferred from the runtime notes' prose, not from a database schema or IaC artifact; confidence on the sensitivity inheritance in finding F1 is accordingly medium.
Whether the IDE client's approval prompt shows full bound parameter values (not just query templates) is assumed from 'shows the SQL' and was not independently verified.

No data was available on actual approval volume, approval accept rate, or whether any logging/monitoring control exists, so detective controls are not scored and consequence reduction via detection was not applied.
